Newborn Care

Bathing and Diapering Your Newborn

Updated: July 1, 2026

Few things feel as high-stakes as the first bath of a slippery, cross newborn , and few become routine as quickly. Babies need far fewer baths than you might think, and diapering becomes muscle memory within days. Here is how to do both safely.

Sponge baths until the cord falls off

Until the umbilical cord stump falls off , usually within one to three weeks , stick to sponge baths so the stump stays dry. Lay your baby on a soft towel in a warm room, and wash one area at a time with a damp cloth, keeping the rest covered and cozy.

Work top to bottom: face first with plain water (no soap near the eyes), then body with a mild baby cleanser if you like, and diaper area last. Pat dry gently, especially in the skin folds.

Moving to tub baths

Once the cord area has healed, you can switch to a baby tub or a clean sink with a few inches of warm water. Support your baby’s head and neck with one arm the whole time and keep a firm hold , wet babies are remarkably slippery.

Two to three baths a week is plenty at this age; more frequent bathing can dry out newborn skin. Daily cleaning of the face, neck folds, hands, and diaper area covers the rest.

Water temperature and bath safety

Aim for comfortably warm water , around body temperature, roughly 37–38°C (about 100°F). Test it with your wrist or elbow, which are more sensitive than fingers, and swirl the water so there are no hot spots.

The unbreakable rule: never leave a baby unattended in water, not even for a few seconds. Gather everything , towel, cleanser, clean diaper, clothes , before the bath starts, and let the phone and doorbell wait.

Diapering, step by step

Set up first: clean diaper open and ready, wipes or damp cloth within reach, one hand always on your baby. Unfasten the dirty diaper, use its front to wipe away the worst, then fold it under your baby while you clean the skin properly.

Wipe front to back , especially important for girls , and clean thoroughly in all the creases. Let the skin dry for a moment, slide the fresh diaper under, and fasten it snugly but not tight; for newborns, fold the front below the cord stump until it falls off.

Expect a lot of these: newborns commonly go through eight to twelve diapers a day. Changing promptly after stools and regularly overall is the single best rash prevention there is.

Preventing and handling diaper rash

Diaper rash is common and usually mild: the fix is frequent changes, gentle cleaning, thorough drying, and a barrier cream with zinc oxide or petroleum jelly at the first sign of redness. A few minutes of diaper-free air time each day helps too.

If a rash is severe, blistered, bleeding, or does not improve after a few days of home care , or comes with fever , check in with your pediatrician, since some rashes (like yeast-based ones) need specific treatment.

Key takeaways

  • Give sponge baths only until the cord stump falls off and heals.
  • Two to three baths a week is enough; test water with your wrist , comfortably warm.
  • Never leave a baby alone in water, even for seconds , prepare everything first.
  • Wipe front to back, dry the creases, and fold diapers below the cord stump.
  • Frequent changes plus barrier cream prevent most diaper rash; see a doctor if it persists.

Frequently asked questions

How often should I bathe my newborn?

Two to three times a week is plenty. Daily baths can dry a newborn’s delicate skin , just clean the face, neck folds, hands, and diaper area daily in between.

What water temperature is safe for a baby bath?

Comfortably warm, around body temperature , roughly 37–38°C (about 100°F). Test with your wrist or elbow and mix the water well so there are no hot spots.

When should I worry about a diaper rash?

See your pediatrician if a rash is severe, blistered, or bleeding, spreads beyond the diaper area, comes with fever, or does not improve after a few days of frequent changes and barrier cream.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
